text: Jovian (/ˈdʒoʊviən/; Latin: Jovianus; Ancient Greek: Ἰοβιανός, romanized: Iobianós; 331 – 17 February 364) was Roman emperor from June 363 to February 364. Born in 331 at Singidunum, Moesia Superior (modern Belgrade, Serbia), he was the son of Varronianus, commander of Constantius II's imperial bodyguards (comes domesticorum). Jovian joined the imperial bodyguard and, in 361, escorted Constantius' remains to the Church of the Holy Apostles. He married Charito and had two sons, Varronianus and another whose name is unknown. In 363, he accompanied Emperor Julian on the Mesopotamian campaign against Shapur II, the Sassanid king. At the Battle of Samarra, Julian was mortally wounded; Ammianus Marcellinus notes that Julian declined to name a successor, fearing he might overlook a worthy candidate or endanger a preferred one. Julian died on 26 June 363. The next day, the army offered the throne to Saturninius Secundus Salutius, praetorian prefect of the Orient, who refused it. Instead, despite Julian's reinstitution of paganism, the army chose the Christian Jovian, a senior officer of the Scholae, as emperor. On the morning of his accession, Jovian resumed the retreat begun by Julian. Though harassed by the Sasanids, the army reached Dura on the banks of the Tigris. Unable to cross the river, Jovian was forced to negotiate a peace treaty on humiliating terms: a thirty-year truce, withdrawal from the five Roman provinces—Arzamena, Moxoeona, Azbdicena, Rehimena, and Corduena—and cession of the fortresses of Nisibis, Castra Maurorum, and Singara to the Sasanids, along with the surrender of Roman interests in Armenia, leaving King Arsaces II without Roman support. The treaty was widely regarded as a disgrace. After crossing the Tigris, Jovian sent an embassy to the West to announce his elevation. With the treaty signed, he and his army marched to Nisibis, where the populace was given three days to leave before the city was handed over to the Sasanids. In September 363, upon arriving at Edessa, Jovian issued two edicts: one limiting the distance a soldier could be sent for straw to signal the end of hostilities, and another restoring estates of the res privata to the Imperial finances after Julian had transferred them to pagan temples. At Antioch in October 363, Jovian faced an enraged populace, with offensive graffiti and insulting authorless bills (famosi) throughout the city, prompting him to order the burning of the Library of Antioch. He left Antioch in November 363, heading for Constantinople, and by December 363 was at Ancyra, where he proclaimed his infant son Varronianus consul. His journey ended on 17 February 364, when he died in his tent at Dadastana, halfway between Ancyra and Nicaea, aged 33. His death, which went uninvestigated, may have resulted from suffocating on poisonous fumes from a brazier in a newly painted bedchamber. Jovian was buried in the Church of the Holy Apostles in Constantinople in a porphyry sarcophagus. He was succeeded by Valentinian I and Valens, who divided the empire between them. To eliminate threats, they blinded Varronianus; according to John Chrysostom, Charito was spared but lived in fear. At Edessa, Jovian was met by bishops, including Athanasius, who had recently returned from exile. The Semi-Arian bishops received a poor reception, while Athanasius delivered a letter insisting on the Nicene Creed and rejecting Arianism. Athanasius was restored to his episcopal duties and allowed to accompany Jovian to Antioch. Upon arrival, Jovian received a letter from the Synod of Antioch requesting the restoration of Meletius as bishop. By September 363, Jovian restored the labarum ("Chi-Rho") as the army's standard, revoked Julian's edicts against Christians, but did not close any pagan temples. He issued an edict of toleration granting full liberty of conscience to his subjects, while banning magic and divination. Despite supporting the Nicene doctrines, he passed no edicts against Arians. Philostorgius, an Arian church historian, stated that Jovian restored churches to their original uses and freed them from the persecutions inflicted by the Apostate Julian. Jovian was consequently the last emperor to rule the entire Roman Empire for the whole of his reign, from his successors Valentinian I and Valens to the fall of the Western Roman Empire, all subsequent administrations involved co-emperors governing a split Eastern and Western jurisdiction.
